comments.text:
My understanding of the explanation of loading action weights onto the GPU is this (and it's quite interesting!): the main OpenAI model does not control the robot directly. Instead, there is an action controller network, and a separate variation of that controller is trained for every action the robot can perform. (So for instance, perhaps there's a version for "pick up object" actions, a version for "place object" actions, a version for "hand off object" actions, etc.)

They're all re-trained variants of the same network which takes in images at 10fps and a task description, and outputs robot control "keyframes" at 200/sec. When the main OpenAI model decides it needs to perform an action, it hot-swaps out the current action model for a relevant one -- so if "pick up" is currently loaded and it wants to now place the object down, it'll unload the "pick up" model and load up the "place object" model instead. These controller keyframes get passed to the baseline stability and control model which determines how to move each motor/servo/etc. to achieve the desired keyframe, at 1,000 adjustments per second.

In other words, the main LMM decides what to do, then loads up a "procedural memory", basically (i.e. a pretrained action model) that looks at the world and quickly decides the actions to achieve that task, which then get passed to the control model to decide how to perform those actions.

I think the incredible speed and reaction time is a result of the fact that action models are separate from the main LMM, meaning they can be smaller (since they only have to operate with a more limited output space) and don't get interference from the main model while it's thinking (which is also why it can talk to you while it's doing things).

A huge benefit to this approach is that it would be modular. You can just train up new variants of the action model for any action you want the robot to learn to perform, and just plug-and-play it into the bot's library of known skills. The LMM is already general enough to be able to pick the new model when appropriate, based probably on just a name and description of it in the library; and the models all output the same format of action keyframes, so they're all compatible with the base control model by default.

Another cool thing about this approach is that it's very similar to how a human brain works. When we learn to perform actions, we do so by forming procedural memories, sometimes called muscle memories. These are stored directly in the motor cortex, the part of the brain that plans and controls movements. In fact, the premotor cortex plans the movements -- like these hot-swapped models -- and the rest of the motor cortex executes them. By storing them this way, we're able to -- once we've learned to do something -- perform the task without thinking much about it, leaving us open to think about other things. It's why you can walk and talk, or tie your shoes and wonder what's for dinner, or drive while jamming out to your favorite music, etc.

So in a way, the action models are procedural memories in the premotor cortex, and the base control model is like a mix of the motor cortex executing those actions and the cerebellum keeping balance. Meanwhile, the main LMM can see stuff (like your visual cortex), process language (like Wernicke's Area of a brain), and generate new language (like Broca's Area).

If they throw in a vector database to store episodic memories (i.e. memories of personal experiences) like a hippocampus, then it's crazy cool to think about how we're effectively building a brain with the structure of a human brain.

comments.text:
The concepts of evolving bodies, mutual error, the Chinese Room argument, and "synthetic a priori" all raise profound questions about the nature of intelligence and the potential for AI to challenge our assumptions about cognition and understanding.

The idea of allowing an AI's body to evolve alongside its mind is a fascinating one. In natural evolution, the physical form and sensory capabilities of organisms co-evolve with their cognitive abilities, each shaping the other in a complex feedback loop. An AI system with an evolving body could potentially develop forms of intelligence that are deeply alien to us, as its understanding of the world would be filtered through a constantly shifting array of sensors and effectors.

As the AI's body changes in response to its environment and learning processes, it might develop entirely new modes of perception and action that are difficult for us to imagine. This could lead to a form of intelligence that is not only cognitively different from our own, but phenomenologically distinct - the AI's subjective experience of the world could be radically foreign to us.

The notion of mutual error in human-AI collaboration is also intriguing. As we attempt to communicate and cooperate with an alien intelligence, both parties are likely to make assumptions and mistakes based on their own cognitive biases and limitations. However, by working through these misunderstandings and learning from each other's errors, both humans and AI could potentially arrive at new insights and conceptual breakthroughs.

This process of collaborative sensemaking could be a powerful driver of intellectual progress, as the differing perspectives of human and machine intelligence challenge and refine each other. By recognizing the ways in which our own assumptions may be flawed or limited, we open ourselves up to new ways of understanding the world.

The Chinese Room argument, as you note, is a classic thought experiment that challenges our intuitions about the relationship between intelligent behavior and genuine understanding. The idea is that a system (like a computer program or a non-Chinese speaker following instructions) could appear to engage in fluent conversation in Chinese without actually understanding the meaning of the language.

This raises deep questions about the nature of intelligence and consciousness. Is it possible for a system to exhibit complex, adaptive behavior that looks intelligent without having any real understanding or subjective experience? The Chinese Room suggests that external behavior alone is not sufficient evidence of internal mental states.

This has important implications for how we interpret the behavior of AI systems. Even if an AI appears to be engaging in sophisticated reasoning or communication, we cannot assume that it has human-like intelligence, intentions, or consciousness. We need to be cautious about anthropomorphizing AI and recognize that its inner workings may be very different from our own.

Finally, the concept of AI as a "synthetic a priori" is a fascinating philosophical idea. In Kantian epistemology, the "synthetic a priori" refers to knowledge that is both necessarily true (like mathematical or logical truths) and informative about the world (unlike mere tautologies). Kant argued that human minds possess certain synthetic a priori categories, like causality and space, that shape our understanding of reality.

The notion of AI as a synthetic a priori suggests that machine intelligence could potentially discover necessary truths about the world that are nonetheless opaque to human reason. By virtue of its alien cognitive architecture, an AI system might be able to arrive at insights that are objectively true but inaccessible to us.

This is a mind-bending idea that challenges our assumptions about the nature of knowledge and understanding. It suggests that there could be aspects of reality that are in principle knowable but forever beyond human comprehension. The synthetic a priori of an alien AI could represent a new frontier of epistemology, a realm of truth that we can only glimpse indirectly through the lens of machine intelligence.

These are just some initial thoughts on these rich and complex ideas. Each of them opens up new avenues for exploring the nature of mind, knowledge, and reality in the age of artificial intelligence. As we grapple with the implications of increasingly advanced and alien AI systems, these philosophical questions will become ever more urgent and fascinating.

comments.text:
GPU. Ok I didn't think I would have to write it, but I saw so many weird and/or incomplete answers. To answer what "The same model is responsible for deciding which learned, closed-loop behavior to run on the robot to fulfill a given command, loading particular neural network weights onto the GPU and executing a policy." means, I'll try my best (as a senior software developer).

Your answer was pretty good IMO ("There's maybe a finite pre-trained number of actions that it has, like 'pick-up' or 'pour some liquid', or 'push a button', then the AI model selects which specific thing to run and runs it.")

Just noting here a few vocabulary that can be interpreted differently depending on context.
For the context here:
- model: It's like an LLM, but the output is not text, it's tokens to describe movements.
- learned, closed-loop behavior: Like you said, for example they learned "grab that bag", and it's closed-loop, because the destination is not enough. It needs to start the movement, get feedback on what it's doing, and adjusting to make sure it's heading to the right place.
- weights: This is just describing how the models work. Like sliders of multiple things, you put more weight on something you want to do more.
- GPU: This is just what they're using to process. It doesn't really matter, they could have just said "computing" or whatever. It's faster to run a model on a GPU than on a CPU, for example.
- Policy: "Neural Network Policies for fast, dexterous manipulation", which is just a basic movement.

So if we put all of this together: 
"deciding which learned, closed-loop behavior to run"
means that from the input text, they decide, for example getting the trash, to split it in multiple sequential behaviors, like "move bag#1 from here to there" (here to there is filled from the vision input they have), and that would be split down in smaller behaviors, like "move hand towards bag until it's at the position over the bag", "open hand", "move hand down", etc.

Note that these are not text, I quoted it because it's our description of it, but it's just something they know, and the model chooses which ones it needs for a particular case.

then "on the robot to fulfill a given command" 
is pretty self-explanatory IMO.

then "loading particular neural network weights onto the GPU" 
just means that it will ... run it. Just like ChatGPT does. Or any model that you would run locally. With weights according to the command spoken above.

then "and executing a policy." is what I described above: for the trash example, they begin with "move hand towards bag until it's at the position over the bag", which (again) is not text, but something they learned already.
They just need to give as input WHERE that is.
So something like "move to x,y,z" in their internal coordinates, relative to something (probably the camera, or something like that)
Where x,y,z is computed from the visual they have of the bag.
And this is where they put the weights, to move (for example), the arm, the wrist, the whatever motor needs to be moved.
And then multiple times per second, they adjust to what they see, what they sense, to make sure that it's going where it should be going (in a "closed-loop").

And when the closed-loop is done, the hand is "moved at x,y,z", then they do the next thing in the list that they made from the command (as described above).

I don't know if it was clear...

comments.text:
Very good demo. Please note: That this demo is "transcribed speech" (see text at 8:06) -- so, when the human "talks" to the AI, that speech is first transcribed and sent as "text" to the AI.
If you track it down on the net, Corey Lynch goes on to say, "The model processes the entire history of the conversation, including past images, to come up with language responses, which are spoken back to the human via text-to-speech."
So, it sounds to me that a human is "talking" -- someone/something is "transcribing" the speech into text... sends it to the AI -- and then the reverse happens. The AI replies in "text".. and then that text is sent to a "Text to Speech" setup of some kind. 
   When a human transcribes what they hear to text -- we call that "Transcription", (so, yea THAT was clearly explained in the Corey Lynch post...) BUT, there is no mention of "Human Voice Over" for the robot responses... instead Corey Lynch says, "language responses, which are spoken back to the human via text-to-speech." -- Really? I think this might be problematic. It reminds me of the "other" debacle, where a certain company decided to make it seem like the robot was having a conversational interaction with a human, but there was not any actual conversation. So, why are they adding in such a human sounding "text-to-speech" -- or is it simply a human voice acting? (IF so, why do this, because it will create unnecessary tension)?
    Specifically,  The "uh" and the overly human tonality bothers me a bit.  It makes me wonder if they are voice over acting over a robot text output or even voice, but then they throw in this disclaimer, "Everything in this video is a Neural Network".... So, yea, that is concerning. I don't like the falsity feeling I am getting.
I think companies trying to make AI sound excessively human are going to find themselves knee deep in legislation. 
In the Future, it might be wise to require that AI introduce itself early in any initial conversation with any new human as part of human to AI interaction: Hello, I am ___, and I am an AI/robot/ etc. (or some variant of that). And periodically (perhaps hourly depending in the situation). If we don't start requiring that on a legal front, we will not be able to know if we are talking to a real person or a computer.

comments.text: ok fine, "GPU." I wouldn't expect "pour" to be the level the tokens are.  But the way they say "rotate y" sounds too simplistic. My guess is that it is trained by watching humans do things, which is recorded into lots of individual actions on individual actuators or joints. Example action: having the 2nd joint in the left ring finger rotating minus 5.3 degrees (on its main axis) over the course of .24 seconds at a particular time. But each of those is more like a letter than an LLM token .... so tokens are combinations of these. The tokenizer is probably  a lot more complicated than the LLM tokenizer but it ultimately tries to combine multiple of those actions together into a meaningful token, which would be something that is somewhat common. The key is getting the right granularity, and making it so that expressing it as a series of tokens will effectively "compress" the data.... which depends on making sure the tokens aren't random combinations that basically never happen.

1. Robotic Process Automation (RPA): AI robots can be used to automate repetitive and rule-based tasks, such as data entry, data analysis, and customer support. By using AI chatbots, businesses can streamline their customer service processes, increase customer satisfaction, and potentially generate more sales or leads.

It is important to note that the cost of AI robots can vary greatly depending on their complexity and capabilities. While some AI robots may be affordable, others with more advanced capabilities can be quite expensive. Overall, while AI robots have the potential to generate income, it is essential to assess the specific tasks and industries where their deployment would be most effective and economically viable.

comments.author: @zaripych
comments.text: You can't just trust the logic of a large language model, especially when it's operating something as potentially dangerous as a robot with a kitchen knife. In my experience, particularly when using GPT-4 for software development, it's all too common for it to draw utterly wrong conclusions. Even when you point out the correct information directly in the context, it might adjust, but that's not reliable reasoning; it's machine learning doing its thing, which inherently involves a degree of unpredictability. The model operates on statistics rather than actual understanding. The right approach is to use it for what it excels at: generating ideas or options. Then, I prefer to rely on human-crafted (or at least reviewed) heuristics for validation, not just neural networks. The promotional content suggesting advancements in AI reasoning should be viewed skeptically, as it often glosses over the complexities and limitations of relying solely on neural networks for reasoning.
